“I’m concerned the production of these chips relies on all sorts of inputs from around the world, including the Gulf, and it’s a fragile ecosystem,” said Sen. TODD YOUNG (R-Ind.). Young was a cosponsor of the $7.4 billion CHIPS and Science Act, which has resulted in a major investment from the South Korean semiconductor supplier SK Hynix Inc. in his state.
There are similar concerns on the other side of the aisle.
Prolonged disruption to the LNG supplies powering Taiwan’s grid threatens the semiconductor supply chain the United States and the global economy depend on,”

said Rep. AMI BERA (D-Calif.), ranking member of the House subcommittee on East Asia and the Pacific. “I’ve been in conversations with our Asian allies, and there is broad agreement that we must reach a resolution before these disruptions worsen.”

TSMC doesn’t anticipate “any significant impact” due to the strait’s closure, but is “monitoring the situation closely,” the company said in a statement Tuesday. Taiwan maintains an LNG “security stockpile” of around 11 days, according to the island’s Ministry of Economic Affairs. Taipei says it’s pivoting to non-Persian Gulf LNG exporters to ensure adequate supplies through April. State-owned Taiwan Power Company is “formulating relevant contingency plans” and said domestic fuel supplies can “withstand short-term international fluctuations,” in a statement Tuesday. The tech industry, which is highly dependent on advanced chips, is not yet worried about a TSMC production crisis, according to venture capitalist ROSS FUBINI. He was an early investor in Anduril and Palantir, which are both working closely with the Pentagon during the current Iran operation. Speaking to NatSec Daily today on the sidelines of the Hill and Valley Forum in Washington, he said, “A company that’s operating at that scale and that level of importance to Taiwan — they will find a way.”
